claims.claim: Ruby only passes data between those calls, which is typically a few milliseconds of a 150–400 ms job
claims.about: Ruby (Sidekiq workers calling libvips and the model)
claims.why: The benchmarks test HTTP servers doing toy work and never measure how much time Ruby spends passing data between calls into native libraries like libvips.

claims.claim: Rewriting the workers in Go or Rust would still call the same libvips and model; it would save something like 5–10% of the CPU time (small gains)
claims.about: Go/Rust vs Ruby for image-processing workers
claims.why: The CPU test shows Go/Rust doing much more pure-language compute than Rails (18–29k vs 3k req/s for fib(20)), but nothing measures a workload where most of the time is spent in native libraries, so the 5–10% estimate can't be checked.

claims.claim: Ruby has a global lock that limits how much Ruby code can run in parallel within one process, so run one Sidekiq process per core
claims.why: Every server ran on 1 CPU, so the measurements can't show how Ruby threads scale across several cores.

claims.claim: Using the jemalloc memory allocator helps Ruby a lot
claims.why: No allocator settings were compared in the measurements.

claims.claim: Moving the tagging part to Python doesn't make anything faster
claims.about: Python vs Ruby for the tagging step
claims.why: In the HTTP tests Python stacks were not faster than Rails (for example, CPU fib: Flask about 1.1k vs Rails 3.1k req/s), which agrees with the claim, but nothing measures model inference in native code.

claims.claim: Long-running Ruby processes grow in memory when handling large images, so restart workers periodically
claims.why: Runs lasted only 15 s on small requests, so memory growth over hours of large-image work isn't measured.
